item.title: A 67-year-old Democratic veteran is becoming the left's favorite to replace Schumer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Progressive lawmakers and activists are hoping to harness momentum from last week’s sweeping Democratic victories to install inspiring new congressional leaders. Many have looked at the Senate and found their guy: a 67-year-old father of three from an affluent Washington suburb who has held public office continuously since 1991. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has emerged as the alternative of choice for a swath of Democrats who believe Chuck Schumer, the longtime Senate Democratic leader, should step aside despite presiding over massive midterm gains. It’s the culmination of a remarkable resurgence for Van Hollen, who spent years inching up the Democratic leadership ladder in the House only to ditch his seniority there for the back benches of the Senate in 2017. Over the past two years, he has emerged as an increasingly strident critic of the Democratic party establishment and its approach to President Donald Trump, as well as its positions on populist economic policies and the U.S. relationship with Israel — and members of the party’s left flank have noticed. A wave of House Democrats, outside activists and even at least one newly elected senator are effectively trying to draft him into what could be an uphill race to unseat the 75-year-old Schumer as majority leader. “I have been very impressed by Senator Van Hollen’s leadership,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who beat a more centrist Democrat in her state’s primary and has said she will not back Schumer. Van Hollen has wavered on whether he is pursuing a role in Senate leadership or perhaps instead a 2028 run for the presidency. He said Tuesday he is “actively listening” as he keeps the door open to a majority leader bid ahead of the early December caucus elections. “I’m trying to talk to our members, and I think it’s important to reach out to everybody,” he said in the Capitol halls. Flanagan said she had not had “formal conversations” with Van Hollen, but another younger Democrat — Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — met with him this week as she called for a leadership shakeup. Outside the building, at a gathering of progressive groups charting an agenda for the coming Democratic majorities, Van Hollen was sharply critical of the existing Senate Democratic power structure — and Schumer in particular. “We just saw democracy in America in action — we should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate,” he said, before later accusing Schumer and the Senate Democratic campaign arm of having “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC” to oppose more progressive candidates in this year’s primaries. That outspokenness has gotten Van Hollen noticed on the left — and it has been especially striking coming from a son of prominent U.S. diplomats who spent decades dutifully rising through the Democratic Party establishment and chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees. “Van Hollen represents a bridge between the old guard — people who’ve been in office for a long time with a more moderate orientation — and the new generation that is coming into office,” said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution. His rhetoric and actions have evolved dramatically, however, since Trump returned to office in 2025. The administration’s spending cuts decimated Van Hollen’s constituency — particularly in his political base of Montgomery County — and his posts on the Appropriations and Foreign Relations committees gave him a front-row seat to Trump’s elimination of USAID. Meanwhile, he became an outspoken critic of the White House’s mass deportation agenda and was the first U.S. lawmaker to visit the El Salvador prison where the administration was sending scores of deportees — including a Maryland man, Kilmar Ábrego García, who had been mistakenly deported in contravention of a court order. Van Hollen has also become increasingly critical of the U.S. posture toward Israel, joining early Democratic pushes to restrict arms sales to Benjamin Netanyahu’s government as its war on Gaza after the 2023 Hamas attacks grew increasingly brutal. “He’s been correct,” said Jeff Cohen, founder of RootsAction, a group pushing its members to back Van Hollen over Schumer. “He’s been with the base of the party on most issues: redefining the U.S.-Israel relationship is one. Taxing the wealthy is another, standing up to AI — all of these issues that Schumer is wrong on.” Van Hollen’s approach to the Senate leadership race has evolved in recent days. He downplayed a bid for top leader earlier this year, including saying in a recent interview that it has “not been my focus.” The day after the election, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed appeared to believe he had passed on a run, calling Van Hollen “my white whale” in response to a question about his ideal Senate leader. But asked about the matter Tuesday as the drumbeat for his candidacy grew, Van Hollen said there should not be a “coronation” for Schumer as he described his ongoing listening tour. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan and as you know, there are many people who think that a change is required,” he said. A Senate aide who was granted anonymity to describe Van Hollen’s thinking said the senator has been influenced by the scale of his party’s midterm victory and the calls he has heard for change — as well as the public outreach he is getting. The aide said Van Hollen is not coordinating the outside effort to nudge him into challenging Schumer. Senate Democrats still broadly expect Schumer to be reelected as leader, and some are openly warning Van Hollen away from jumping into the race. “I'm going to vote for Schumer. He helped recruit a great class, and I can't imagine why you would vote for someone like Van Hollen with no record of doing anything,” pro-Israel Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) told reporters. Asked about whether Van Hollen will run, Fetterman added, “I dare him to.” Schumer’s backers point to his decades of fundraising experience, deep well of relationships within the caucus and across the party, and his work to unite his colleagues and battle Trump over the past year. And with Democrats poised to pick up as many as nine seats — a once-unthinkable outcome — they are questioning why senators would depose the leader who helped make it happen. "When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said Tuesday at a joint news conference with Schumer. But those arguments are carrying little water with those who view Schumer as out of touch with the direction of the party. They note that while he supported the incoming freshmen with hundreds of millions of dollars of general-election spending, he opposed some of them during the primary. Van Hollen could be using his flirtations with a bid to influence some end-of-year decisionmaking. He is pushing Congress to cut off Iran war funding as they head toward a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, and he wants a provision mandating cooperation with Israel stripped from the annual defense policy bill. Those stances could help push Schumer and the party into a more confrontational posture, which Van Hollen signaled he wanted in an interview earlier this year. “It’s going to be very important that Democrats let voters know not only what we’re against but what we stand for,” he said. “And I think a lot of voters, you know, think Democrats have been too much finger-in-the-wind. They’ve been too wishy-washy.” Grace Yarrow and Lisa Kashinsky contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/11/chris-van-hollen-senate-leader-01160588

item.title: Alaska judge rules Mary Peltola's request for ballot data in Senate race is 'not reasonable'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — An Alaska judge ruled Wednesday that a request by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign for a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected is “not reasonable,” particularly given the time crunch election officials face as they continue counting ballots from last week's election. Ballots are still being tallied in the ranked vote election, in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Alaska’s is the only Senate race in the country that remained too early to call. The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That date is also the Division of Elections’ target for conducting ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes. Attorneys for Peltola’s campaign last Friday sued state elections officials, seeking a list of voters whose absentee ballots have been rejected and the reasons for the rejections. They said their intent was to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. But attorneys for the state said the information requested would violate voter privacy. They also said producing such a list from a voter database would constitute an “electronic service or product” that under state law may not take priority over an agency's main responsibilities. Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews, in a written ruling, said that “in theory” records from the voter database could be redacted and produced in a way that would allow their release. But he said the division is not required to disclose the records requested by the campaign because they “cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information.” The division has deadlines to meet and says its staff is working long hours to accomplish the agency's “fundamental responsibility” of administering elections, he wrote. “The timing of the Campaign's request could simply not be worse,” Matthews wrote. An email seeking comment from one of the law firms representing Peltola's campaign was not immediately returned Wednesday, which was a holiday. The state Department of Law, which represented the Division of Elections, in a statement said it was pleased with Matthews' decision. Abha Khanna, an attorney for Peltola’s campaign, said during arguments Tuesday before Matthews the campaign wasn’t seeking to disrupt the ballot counting process. She said the absentee ballot review process was going “incredibly smoothly.” But Khanna argued the information sought is a matter of public record and in line with what campaign observers have access to in locations where absentee review boards are meeting. The campaign wanted access to that information in a more centralized way, she said. Attorneys for the state have argued that reports generated by the division with lists of ballots to be reviewed during the absentee ballot review process are not public records because they contain confidential information and are “ephemeral working documents that are not meant for preservation.” Michaela Thompson, who oversees the absentee ballot review boards for the division, said in an affidavit that the version of the report received by observers of the review process — including those affiliated with the campaigns — does not include as much confidential information but does include home addresses that many voters seek to keep private. The observers sign confidentiality agreements and cannot keep, copy or record information in the report, she said. The division’s “old, inflexible” database cannot produce a report that excludes confidential addresses, meaning the agency would have to work with a vendor to create a more tailored report, Thompson said. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/alaska-judge-rules-request-peltola-000233622.html

item.title: Hegseth's group reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A US Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier admonished Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage Wednesday after some in the group laughed and talked near the solemn memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!” the sentinel called out, stopping his patrol to face the group as they departed - CNN A US Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanded Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a group of his senior advisers Wednesday after some in the group laughed and talked near the solemn memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel called out, stopping his patrol to face the group as they departed. Hegseth was standing and taking photos in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser and deputy assistant Tami Radabaugh after the ceremony held at Arlington National Cemetery for Veterans Day. Some in the group were laughing and chatting after taking photos, prompting the soldier patrolling in front of the Tomb to yell out and correct them. When asked for comment, Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.” “The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is one of the most sacred war memorials in the US, marking the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I. A soldier assigned to The Old Guard, or 3rd Infantry Regiment, has been guarding the tomb around the clock, rain or shine, since 1948. Foreign dignitaries, presidents, public figures and politicians frequently visit the Tomb to pay their respects to American service members. Hegseth and his team were at Arlington National Cemetery for a ceremony that was also attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. The defense secretary had been under renewed scrutiny and pressure in recent days after articles of impeachment were filed against him by outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie. But in a procedural vote on Tuesday night, the GOP successfully blocked the impeachment process from moving forward, prompting Hegseth and his allies to claim vindication. Hegseth stood accused by Massie of executing unlawful orders, including by waging war in Iran without congressional approval, ignoring laws about minimizing civilian casualties, and directing the Pentagon to carry out extrajudicial killings. In a press conference on Tuesday, Hegseth said the charges amounted to a policy dispute and not high crimes and misdemeanors. President Donald Trump, who also faced criticism for behavior at Arlington National Cemetery when he filmed a campaign video there in 2024, stood by Hegseth leading up to Tuesday’s vote and vowed to continue supporting him moving forward. This story has been updated with additional information. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/11/politics/hegseth-reprimanded-guard-tomb-unknown-soldier

item.title: 'I kept the faith:' Democrat Scott Colom flips Mississippi Senate seat in historic upset
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday to flip another Senate seat for Democrats and become the first Black candidate elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi in more than 140 years. According to figures from the Associated Press, Colom — who will also be Mississippi’s first Black senator since 1989 — won 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith finished with 48.7%. “There were times that I couldn't get donors to answer the phone,” Colom told supporters as they celebrated his historic upset late Wednesday night . “They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith.” Mississippi — one of the reddest states in the country — wasn't really on the national radar prior to Nov. 3. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a “likely Republican” hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it . But by the end of Election Night, Colom and Hyde-Smith were separated by just 65 votes, shocking the nation. Colom’s win expands Democrats' total number of Senate seats to 55 and cements the party’s best overall midterm performance since 1974 — a rout that has seen the GOP lose control of the Senate, the House and statehouses across the country . As lawyers, operatives and legal observers descended on Mississippi to watch officials count every last ballot, Colom repeatedly expressed confidence that his campaign would prevail, flooding the airwaves and attending at least eight post-election events. "It's very clear the direction of this," he told reporters on Friday . Colom picked up that thread in Wednesday’s victory speech. “I've been telling everybody that we're going to win this election,” he said. “I was saying it 8 or 9 months ago. But every time I said it, I pointed out that people were going to give me too much credit for it because it's not something that I did. It's something that we did. All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this. I had the courage to believe in Mississippi.” Hyde-Smith conceded to Colom in a video posted on X Wednesday evening : "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state." Alaska is now the only undecided Senate race. Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan 48.9% to 47.3% with 84% of the vote counted, according to the latest AP figures. Who is Scott Colom? Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus. In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases. Colom gives an update about his Senate race on Nov. 4, 2026 in Jackson, Miss. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination. "I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times . But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ." In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper." Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy. How Colom won Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since. There were signs before Election Day that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%. Hyde-Smith speaks at a campaign event in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. Madison Thorn/Bloomberg via Getty Images Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn. Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from." In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 19 million views on Colom's X account . She done lost her damn mind. pic.twitter.com/wHPt4PSAob — Scott Colom (@scott_colom) October 13, 2026 When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own). In the end, it wasn't enough to get Hyde-Smith over the line. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom attended his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices. "I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/mississippi-senate-results-scott-colom-narrowly-defeats-cindy-hyde-smith-flipping-another-seat-for-democrats-in-midterm-elections-232119638.html

item.title: Famed ship heads for afterlife as artificial reef in deliberate sinking off Florida
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Gorman Nov 11 (Reuters) - Famed ocean liner SS United States, the largest passenger ship ever built in America and the world's fastest, headed for the sea floor near Florida on Wednesday in a deliberate sinking designed to transform the vessel into the world's biggest artificial reef. The finale to a ‌yearlong process preparing the ship to meet its destiny, 75 years after it was first launched at sea, was presented in a livestream with aerial views of ‌the once-grand vessel's rusted hulk, stripped of its two smokestacks, quietly, slowly settling into calm waters of the Gulf of Mexico before succumbing to the deep. The ship, measuring nearly 1,000 feet (300 m) from stem to stern, was ​surrounded by onlookers and safety crews aboard dozens of tugboats and recreational vessels that accompanied the ocean liner as it was towed out to sea for its final voyage. By then, work crews had spent months removing all environmentally unsafe materials from the ship, including residual fuel, wiring, glass, ductwork and other non-metal items, as well as any objects that could pose entanglement hazards for scuba divers. The crews then cut holes strategically throughout the ship's hull and its decks to ensure that it would sink in a gradual, level and uniform manner, according to a fact sheet ‌posted online by project organizers. No explosives were used. Passageways were ⁠also cut through the 12 decks of the interior to allow for marine life to thrive in and around the ship on the sea floor. If all goes as planned, the aging 20th-century vessel will come to rest upright on the gulf floor at a depth of 180 ⁠feet off the coast of Destin, Florida, a resort town and recreational fishing haven known for its white sand beaches and emerald green waters. The upper deck is expected to end up about 50 feet beneath the surface, organizers said. SINKING STARTS SLOWLY The sinking process began at about 1 p.m. CST but was so imperceptibly slow that the majority of the ocean liner's hull remained well above the surface ​as ​the sun set on the idle ship, surrounded by blinking lights of nearby vessels. After hours, during which ​the waterline was seen creeping up the ship's hull inches at a ‌time, the sinking accelerated as the sea poured through the holes cut into the lower decks and flooded the interior. In the final moments, livestream footage showed the ship abruptly listing to its port side before gently rolling into the sea and disappearing. Warren Jones, a spokesperson for organizers, who watched the sinking from an observation boat, said the SS United States would probably take 30 to 60 minutes to reach the seabed once the interior compartments were all completely filled with water. The SS United States, a wonder of post-World War Two oceanic luxury and engineering that carried the rich and famous across the Atlantic at speeds still unmatched, was retired from service in 1969 amid the rising popularity of commercial air travel. The ‌vessel sat moored for nearly 30 years in Philadelphia, seemingly destined to be sold for scrap, before ​authorities in Okaloosa County, in Florida's panhandle, stepped in to purchase the ship as part of a $13 million ​project. "We worked year after year to keep that ship from going to the ​scrap yard," said Jones, a boyhood passenger of the ship and representative of the SS United States Conservancy, a group that sold the ship ‌to Okaloosa County. After obtaining permission from the US Coast Guard and other ​agencies, the county had the vessel towed to ​a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, where it was prepared for disposal at sea. The SS United States will be in good company, joining a collection of more than 500 smaller underwater sites created from the remains of various sunken ships and concrete structures to create a divers' haven known as the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Artificial Reefs. Speaking ​with Reuters by phone on Wednesday night, Jones said some wreck ‌divers were already gearing up to explore the sunken remnants of the ocean liner as early as Thursday morning. Jones, recounting vivid memories of riding the ship ​as an 8-year-old passenger with his family in 1961, said he was "comforted seeing it settle on the floor of the gulf and being embraced by ​the sea." (Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Stephen Coates and Tom Hogue) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/famed-ship-heads-afterlife-artificial-003800609.html

item.title: Brooklyn building collapse leaves at least 2 people dead; rescue operations ongoing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
At least two people are dead and over a dozen others injured after a building collapsed in Brooklyn, according to New York City authorities. A "dangerous" search and rescue operation is ongoing and there could be more victims, fire officials warned. A three-story building at the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford Avenues in the Flatbush neighborhood collapsed into an adjacent excavation site, where workers were on scene, according fire officials. The wall of another three-story building that now stands next to the site was also shorn off, exposing apartments. "This was a major technical response," FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said at a press briefing. "Multiple people from the building and a construction site were trapped." Angelina Katsanis/Reuters - PHOTO: Emergency personnel work at the scene of a partial building collapse where, according to local reports, people are trapped in Brooklyn, Nov. 11, 2026. Two people have died, according to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Another 17 people were injured, including four in critical condition, 12 in stable and a firefighter with minor injuries, Bonsignore said. The victims include seven children, Bonsignore said, without specifying if they were among the deceased. It is unclear how many people may still be missing in the collapse, Bonsignore said, saying it will be a "prolonged operation" and that they expect there to be more victims. "This was a devastating collapse," Mamdani said at the press briefing. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters - PHOTO: Emergency personnel work at the scene of a partial building collapse in Brooklyn, Nov. 11, 2026. Earlier, the FDNY said several construction workers were being transported to the hospital for treatment, and firefighters were trying to get a count of all the workers on the job site. Excavation work had been underway at the construction site, which has been approved for a three-story building, officials said. Plans for a nine-story, mixed-use building there had yet to be approved, officials said. The cause of the collapse remains under investigation by the Department of Buildings and law enforcement, authorities said. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images - PHOTO: Members of the FDNY respond to the scene of a partial building collapse, Nov. 11, 2026, in Brooklyn. The first 911 call on the collapse came in at 4:01 p.m., according to the FDNY. Firefighters could be seen among the debris in the construction pit. After several hours, search-and-rescue canines could also be seen at work. Mamdani called the rescue operation "incredibly challenging" as crews navigated "precarious wreckage." "The units are performing dangerous and heroic work," Bonsignore said. Amid the massive response, at least two people could be seen being rescued from the rubble, pulled out on stretchers. In one dramatic scene, a woman was rescued more than two hours into the rescue operation, as night fell on the site. A man who had been frantically looking for his pregnant wife told reporters, "I have an update from my wife, she is alive," before boarding an ambulance with a victim. WABC - PHOTO: Firefighters carry a person on a stretcher after they were pulled out of a collapsed building in Brooklyn, Nov. 11, 2026. The NYC Department of Buildings said its inspectors "are on scene at a major building collapse near Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn assisting with recovery operations and conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings." NYC Council Member Farah Louis, who represents Flatbush, called the images from the site "heartbreaking." Ryan Murphy/AP - PHOTO: First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York, Nov. 11, 2026. "We are devastated to learn that at least one life has been lost, with multiple people reported trapped and several injured as emergency personnel work urgently to reach everyone in the rubble," Louis said in a statement. "My immediate priority is the safety of everyone impacted, and my team is actively working to reach affected families to connect them with critical information and support during this frightening time," the statement continued. Mamdani urged people to avoid the area amid the rescue response. "As emergency operations continue, please join me in holding our neighbors and the members of this community in our hearts," he said in a statement. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/rescue-operations-underway-after-building-collapses-brooklyn-new/story?id=138059620

item.title: Democrats frustrated by absences in failed Hegseth impeachment vote
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
From left: Nancy Pelosi, Steven Horsford and Haley Stevens missed the vote on Tuesday evening. Composite: Getty Images, Bloomberg Democratic lawmakers expressed outrage at nearly a dozen of their colleagues for missing a vote Tuesday evening to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , allowing Republicans to defeat the effort. Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort , which failed by just seven votes. Some blamed traffic and conflicting events and others accused Speaker Mike Johnson of closing the vote early. Many of those not in the Capitol said they support the effort to impeach Hegseth. “You should show up and do your job,” Abdul El-Sayed , the senator-elect of Michigan, said on CNN to the Democratic lawmakers Tuesday. Richard Ojeda, the representative-elect of North Carolina, told CNN that the Democratic representatives “failed” by not voting. “Shame on them for not showing up,” Ojeda said on Tuesday. “I mean, this is important … they had an opportunity to finally get rid of this buffoonery we had.” The missing Democrats gave House Republicans the numbers to shelve the impeachment effort by voting 211 – 204 to refer eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a House committee. Speaking at Arlington national cemetery to mark Veterans Day, Donald Trump praised Hegseth and said he had done a “fantastic job” as the Pentagon head. “I had a feeling that was going to happen,” the president said of the failed effort to impeach Hegseth, adding: “He loves you, and he protects you – he’s all about you.” The articles, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie , included charges of violating congressional authority by waging war in Iran . The effort came after voters overwhelming cast ballots for Democratic candidates in the 2026 midterms, largely in rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies – including the war in Iran. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a representative from California, told MeidasTouch there was “no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues”. “This is what the people have been talking about … so shame on folks who were not here because these people lost,” Kamlager-Dove added. Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico wrote on X that she was “blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due to a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote”. “When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out. She immediately filed a report of her vote of ‘NO’ to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record,” Stansbury wrote, adding that Hegseth “must be impeached now”. Laura Gillen of New York similarly wrote on X she too was stuck in traffic but “strongly” believes Hegseth should be impeached. Jonathan Jackson, of Illinois, wrote on X that he also was stuck behind the traffic jam. Brittany Pettersen of Colorado wrote on X that she was “denied” the ability to vote. Member of Pettersen’s office later told 9News she too was stuck in traffic. Julia Brownley of California wrote on Facebook that Johnson “closed the vote” before she could make it to the House floor. “As I and many of my colleagues were rushing to the floor to support Hegseth’s impeachment, Mike Johnson closed the vote before we could,” Brownley wrote. Marilyn Strickland of Washington also missed the vote by one minute because she was stuck behind a motocade, but that she would have voted to impeach Hegseth, Strickland’s office told Politico . Nancy Pelosi of California missed the vote because she was in San Francisco to meet with local veterans and accept a Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award, Pelosi’s spokesperson told SFGate . Lou Correa of California wrote on Instagram that he was undergoing a medical procedure and remaining in his district until he was medically cleared. Steven Horsford of Nevada, Haley Stevens of Michigan and Frederica Wilson of Florida did not provide public reasons for their absence on Tuesday. Several Democratic lawmakers who did vote on the effort to impeach Hegseth noted that they were also busy with other life events but still made their way to the Capitol. Pat Ryan of New York wrote on X that he was recovering from back surgery but left the hospital early in order to cast his vote. Congressman Glenn Ivey, a Maryland Democrat, called the absence of the 11 lawmakers during Tuesday’s vote “certainly disappointing”, but said there would be “other chances” to advance impeachment efforts. In an interview, Ivey said he was “absolutely” supportive of renewing the push when Democrats regain control of both chambers in January. At the same time, he argued that voters made clear that concerns about the cost of living remain their top priority. “There aren’t a lot of people, in my district anyway, [whose ability] to stay in their house depends on whether Hegseth gets impeached or not,” Ivey said. “We’ve been calling it the affordability agenda, but I think for many people, it’s really a survivability agenda, and we need to be focused on that.” • This story was updated on 11 November 2026.
